article.title: Revolution and Fun in France - YDSA
article.content: France’s ongoing student uprisings have featured music, aura battles, combativeness and joyous celebration. To build a socialist movement in the US, we need to understand our biggest material barriers to revolutionary joy. “J’ai deux passions: la fanfare, la révolution” I have two passions: the marching band, the revolution “Vive les blocages, les sabotages” Long live the blockades, the sabotages “Les ZAD et les manifs sauvages!” The ZADs and the riots! -French Protest Anthem Protestors in costume (left) facing off with riot police (right), (October 31st, Wikimedia Commons ) Over the past two months, workers and youth have risen up across Europe , with their agitation spreading to parts of South America, Asia , and even Canada . While it is not the aim of this article, nor within its scope, to discuss the implications of these events for the young socialist movement here in the United States, the demonstrations from France offer one very important takeaway: They are having fun. This may sound like an insignificant detail, but if we want to achieve mass mobilization on a similar scale in our own communities, and if we want to go beyond the energy of our previous rebellions, then we have to understand why we are currently materially unable to . So let’s look into the revolutionary joy of the masses in France – through chants and bands, aura and militancy – as well as how we can get to their level ourselves. Good Chants and Music The rain sprinkles onto Place de la République . You stand, surrounded on all sides by a sea of your comrades, waiting in anticipation. Then, it begins – trumpets, drums, violins, cymbals, all a wall of noise – but this isn’t any ordinary concert. It’s playing songs reminiscent of long battles, drawing from your community’s decades-long history of struggle. Bella Ciao . The Internationale . Even some pop-culture rebel music from Star Wars and The Hunger Games. A new crowd favorite, J’ai Deux Passions , brings everyone into chorus: One of the most defining features of the protests in France was this abundance of wonderful noise. Not only have there been creative chants, but there’s been whole bands and orchestras out on the streets, in the squares, and they’ve even spread to Spain . The ability to have mass, collective participation in music stems from the united, revolutionary base of the multiracial French working-class – where amidst this diverse proletariat, everyone’s on the same page, with common interest and solidarity in the face of repression. This can be contrasted with the examples of reformist, white, and liberal No Kings protesters here in the United States, who in many places just walked down the street and chatted to themselves or stayed silent, maybe doing one or two half-hearted call-and-responses. Aura Masked demonstrator strikes a pose in front of a burning dumpster (October 17th, Instagram) The aura of an uprising can come from a variety of sources. As previously mentioned, you can start a chant or play an instrument. You can get on top of something and wave a flag. You can take photos in front of some burning stuff. You can look out and see thousands of people with you, all marching as one. Or, you can have an aura battle . Aura battles and their predecessors, dance and rap battles, have been around for decades under various names. In France, they’ve been one of the biggest ways working-class kids have begun their political involvement these last few months. This is because aura battles are a youth cultural practice that, though at first non-political, are a form of collective organization that can lead into political work. Just like socialists in 19th-century Germany pieced together a working-class sport and art culture , so too have young revolutionaries in France pieced together their working-class culture by providing an organizing infrastructure for collective activities like aura battles, music, and more. As young socialists in the US, we should look to intervene in our own youth and working-class culture, using joy and solidarity as a deterrent against both reactionary social behaviors and as a tactic of revolutionary organization. Militancy One of the biggest things that makes taking to the street fun is becoming unstoppable. Those of us who were around during the George Floyd Uprising, or during certain high-intensity pro-Palestine and anti-ICE struggles in the years following, know the thrill of having a protest “pop off”. We take the streets, become a force, and don’t let anyone stop us. Every day we spend fearful of, and in submission to the cops makes moments like these feel that much better. Young protestors atop the Monument à la République in Paris (October 17th, Wikimedia Commons ) In France, much like the US in 2020, youth and students have held the line, forced police to retreat, and asserted their power despite repression by the brutalizing, heavy-handed CRS (French National Police) . Their boldness has imbued the movement with a revolutionary character and has exploded the contradiction between the workers and the capitalist state. Now let me make this clear before you get any ideas: militancy must be born OF the people, not imposed upon them. If we jump the gun and act recklessly, or take a commandist approach over the movement, we risk alienating ourselves from our communities. We also risk becoming walking targets for an incredibly repressive judicial system , and causing harm to those we are trying to protect. We’ll get to the fun stuff when the workers have built an organizing infrastructure and movement that can support it. Why Not Here? The reason that France, Europe, and parts of South America are in revolt while we’re stuck either watching from the sidelines or being preoccupied with “fixing the system from within” isn’t due to any metaphysical difference between us and them – it’s due to our material conditions. The fragmentation and atomization of the proletariat and the breakdown of our basic socialization processes, especially in the years following the Covid-19 Pandemic, have been the primary contributors to our lack of joyous revolutionary struggle. We can’t simply rely on broad analysis, apparently easy answers, or smooth-talking populist politicians – we should take seriously the horror that this question implies: Why have we stopped playing in our moments where liberation seems possible? On another note, Y/DSA and other left-wing organizations, as they exist today, are often composed not of the multiracial proletariat, but rather the white downwardly-mobile petit-bourgeoise or “middle class” . Radicalized by the rapidly-declining benefits of life in the imperial core, these college-educated workers form the basis for a movement which, while good-intentioned, often inadvertently seeks to restore their benefits looted from the Global South and internal colonies. The Medicare for All, College for All, Green New Deal, and Tax the Rich campaigns generally exemplify this tendency . DSA 2021 Member Survey Report ( 2021 ) If we want to be like the French youth and achieve revolutionary joy through uprising, we must work to develop a revolutionary struggle that seeks to destroy the capitalist state itself, not just ask it to be nicer to us. YDSA members should attempt to support the organization of non-white and non-student youth, who both make up a majority of 18-24 year-olds, in their workplaces, schools, and neighborhoods. Only by addressing the crisis of proletarian disorganization can it become possible to rise up en masse against our capitalist enemies. Always remember that we are beginners — we have so much to learn and so many ways to grow as socialists. In the struggle for a better and dare I say more France-like world, the best time to get started was yesterday, the second best time is now! Manny Heffley “Revolt” graffiti from George Floyd Uprising (2020, Unknown )
